title: 'Open' to Whom? — Washington's Open-Strait Claim vs. a 90% Traffic Collapse
narrative: President Trump said Monday that no talks with Iran were taking place or scheduled 'and he insisted that the Strait of Hormuz was open.' U.S. Central Command says 'despite Iranian aggression, the Strait of Hormuz remains open for commercial vessel traffic.' Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority says the strait 'remains blocked and will not be reopened until Iran's conditions are accepted.' The argument is over a word. The shipping data describes something else entirely: a waterway that moved three registered commercial ships on Sunday, down roughly 90% from the ~130 ships a day that crossed before the war.
telemetry: Kpler AIS/shipping data: 3 ships transited Sunday Aug 16; 5 on Saturday Aug 15, with none registered for Sunday (Reuters)
5-day average ~12 transits vs ~130 ships/day before the war began Feb 28 — roughly a 90% drop (CNBC analysis of Kpler data)
CBS News tracked just three commercial ships transiting Tuesday; the Joint Maritime Information Center said commercial traffic fell to a three-week low
Lloyd's List analysis: between July 13-19, only two ships used the U.S.-backed southern route hugging Oman's coast — BOTH transited with AIS transponders switched off ('dark')
IMO (U.N.): at least 61 attacks on commercial vessels in the strait since Feb 28; 17 mariners killed
CENTCOM itself acknowledged Iran launched 30+ attacks 'endangering hundreds of innocent mariners'

Marisks CEO Dimitris Maniatis (CBS): 'nothing is going through' for large ocean-going, internationally owned merchant vessels; U.S. air-support convoys are 'definitely not enough' — ships still being hit in the southern corridor
Greek shipping giant Dynacom — one of the last international operators willing to transit — had two ships struck off Oman, forcing crew evacuations
South Korea's Sinokor Group is offering mariners six months of extra pay for a return voyage through the strait (Bloomberg via CBS)
CNN (this week, citing a tracking firm): 'Over 80% of ships now bypass Iran's preferred route' through the strait
Iran's top military command (Khatam al-Anbiya): the only 'safe' route is the northern lanes through Iranian waters; ships using the U.S.-recommended Omani route have been attacked (BBC)
Trump (Aug 17, as the 60-day U.S.-Iran ceasefire MOU expires): threatened to 'bomb the s--- out of' Oman if the Gulf nation 'gets in the way' of a Hormuz deal
analysis:
The word 'open' has become the most contested piece of maritime vocabulary in the world, and both sides are using it as a political claim rather than a description of the water. The data that matters — AIS transits, insurer behavior, crew willingness — says the strait is functionally closed to normal commerce even as it remains physically traversable.

What the official claims actually assert: CENTCOM says the strait 'remains open for commercial vessel traffic.' Technically, that is true — vessels can and do transit, and a handful do every day. But the qualifier does the work. The relevant question is not whether the waterway can be crossed. It is whether commercial shipping treats it as a usable route. The answer, from every independent measure, is no.

Kpler's numbers are the cleanest version of the story: three registered transits on Sunday, five on Saturday with none registered Sunday, a five-day average around twelve against a pre-war baseline of roughly 130. That is not a slowdown. That is a collapse of about 90% of the traffic that made the strait the world's most important energy chokepoint. A route that loses nine-tenths of its traffic is not 'open' in any commercial sense — it is a war zone that a few operators still dare to cross.

The behavior of the operators who do cross is the second layer of evidence. Lloyd's List found that the only two ships to use the U.S.-backed southern route in the week of July 13-19 both ran with their AIS transponders off. Dark transits are what ships do when they want to hide from attackers — or from the record. A route whose users switch off their identification systems is not a route operators trust. It is a route they gamble on.

Insurers and crews have made their assessment without any political framing. War-risk insurance on the route is roughly 40 times pre-crisis levels. Sinokor is offering six months of extra pay for a single return voyage. Dynacom, one of the last major international operators willing to attempt transits, had two ships struck off Oman in the same period. The maritime industry has priced the strait as a war zone. That price is the market's verdict on 'open.'

The geography of the remaining traffic is the third layer, and it undercuts both Washington and Tehran. The only corridor with meaningful traffic is the northern route through Iranian waters, run by Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority — which demands permits and has declared no vessel may pass without one. CNN reports over 80% of ships now bypass the Iranian-preferred route entirely. So the 'open' strait is one where the residual traffic is split between a dangerous southern corridor and an Iranian-administered northern one, with most of the world's fleet avoiding both.

Then there is the death toll. The IMO counts at least 61 attacks on commercial vessels in the strait since February 28 and 17 mariners killed. CENTCOM itself acknowledges 30+ Iranian attacks. Seventeen dead seafarers is the human denominator of the entire argument — the reason insurers charge 40x, the reason crews demand hazard pay, the reason Sunday had zero registered transits.

Both governments are issuing claims that function as propaganda. Washington's 'open' is technically defensible and functionally false. Tehran's 'blocked' is functionally closer to the lived experience of shipping while being physically false. The gap between the rhetoric on both sides and the AIS record is the story. The ships are the data, and the data shows a strait that the world's commercial fleet has, in large part, already abandoned.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: 'Open' is a political claim, not a maritime fact. AIS data shows commercial traffic down ~90% from the ~130 ships/day pre-war baseline, with three registered transits on Sunday and the two ships on the U.S.-backed route running dark. The industry has already priced the verdict: war-risk insurance ~40x pre-crisis, crews offered six months' extra pay for one voyage, and 17 mariners dead since February. CENTCOM's 'remains open for commercial vessel traffic' is technically true and functionally false — and Iran's 'blocked' is the mirror image. The ships tell the real story.
